options: Data that is used only occasionally
Data older than the retention policy allows
questions.explanation: The definition given is that data which is not utilised is Dark Data.

questions.stem: Why is Dark Data typically not in use, and how does this affect its status as an asset?
options: It is in use but too expensive to store, so it is an asset
It has been deleted, so it is no longer an asset
It is not in use due to a lack of technology, and it is not a Data Asset
It is fully utilised but poorly documented, so it is a liability
It is in use only for marketing, so it is a partial asset
questions.explanation: Dark Data sits unused because the technology to exploit it was lacking or too expensive, and for that reason it is not a Data Asset.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines Dormant Data?
options: Data that can never be analysed
Data that must be purged immediately
Data that is still being loaded into the warehouse
Data that is usable but underutilised, because decision-makers do not use it or it is not currently required for analysis
questions.explanation: Dormant Data is usable data that is underutilised: decision-makers do not use it or it is not needed for analysis at present, but it cannot simply be deleted.

questions.stem: Where is Dormant Data typically kept?
options: In the operational database alongside live data
On tape drives, in Hadoop or, nowadays, in Object Storage
In the data warehouse serving layer
In application memory for quick access
questions.explanation: Because Dormant Data cannot be deleted or purged, it is kept on tape drives, in Hadoop and increasingly in Object Storage.

questions.stem: Before the introduction of Big Data, roughly what percentage of data was Dark Data?
questions.explanation: Around 90% of data was Dark before Big Data, since it included semi-structured and unstructured datasets and sometimes structured data as well.

questions.stem: Before Big Data technologies, what was the only reason companies kept datasets such as logs, JSON, XML, video and audio files?
questions.explanation: The technologies to analyse such data were absent or too expensive, so companies retained it only for compliance or audit purposes.

questions.stem: Which example is given of data becoming Dormant?
options: Customer buying and spending data from before January 2020 after the Covid-19 changes in behaviour
Server logs that were never parsed
Video files that no tool could analyse
Duplicate customer records created by a migration
questions.explanation: Covid-19 changed buying and spending behaviour so much that pre-January 2020 data became Dormant for marketing and campaigning in most organisations.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed among the technologies and frameworks companies invest in to make use of Dark Data?
questions.explanation: The investments named are Data Lake, Delta Lake, Lakehouse, Data Vault, Business Vault, HDFS, Object Storage and NoSQL databases; mainframes are not among them.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between the amount of Dark Data in an organisation and cost?
options: Dark Data is free to hold because it is never processed
The more Dark Data, the more cost without any return on investment
Dark Data reduces cost by replacing structured storage
Cost falls as Dark Data grows because it is compressed
Dark Data costs are always recovered through compliance fines avoided
questions.explanation: More Dark Data means more cost with no ROI, which is why a CDO should keep it as low as possible.

questions.stem: What is predicted to become the most essential and obvious KPI for a Chief Data Officer?
questions.explanation: Dark Data Management is expected to become the key KPI for a CDO, since Dark Data represents cost without return.
